regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY looks unimpeachable until you note that the RBI's own forecast sits at 6.7% YoY — a 110bps gap that historically reflects deflator assumptions, not real output divergence. PMI Composite at 55.9 is genuine, but core sector at 4.8% YoY (down from 5.0%) and IIP overall at 8.0% YoY suggest the goods economy is running cooler than the services PMI implies. The quality of growth is services-led and credit-fuelled — both are fine until the funding side of credit tightens.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY is the wrong number to watch; core CPI at 3.9% YoY is the right one, and the gap between them is entirely fuel (22.93% YoY, 95th percentile) and food (7.74% YoY, rising two consecutive months). The inversion: if RBI holds the repo at 5.25% p.a. while WPI runs at 9.92% YoY and fuel inflation is at a 10-year high, the real policy rate for producers is already negative — that is not a pause, it is passive easing into an inflation overshoot.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Credit at 19.4% YoY against deposits at 17.8% YoY sounds manageable until you note that the 160bps divergence has widened for two consecutive months and the CD ratio at 81% sits at the 73rd percentile historically. The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% while the repo was on hold, the eventual correction came through risk-weight tightening on unsecured lending — the RBI's playbook is well-worn. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile, rising two straight months) is the segment to watch: it is where the next macro-prudential circular lands.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is steady, but the real rate against headline CPI is just 29bps — against WPI it is negative. The RBI's own inflation forecast has moved up to 5.1% YoY from 4.6%, which means the committee is watching the same fuel and food data the market is. A cut is not priced and should not be; the more interesting question is whether the next move is a hike disguised as a macro-prudential measure on credit risk weights rather than a rate action.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, up from 75.6%) confirm the investment cycle is real, not budgetary fiction. The inversion: utilisation above 75% is the threshold at which private capex historically accelerates — India is there, which is why vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY and services credit at 24.3% YoY are both surging. The risk is that deposit-constrained banks begin rationing credit to capex borrowers before the cycle matures.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month (73rd percentile) is solid but not accelerating — the month-on-month dip from ₹2,00,640 cr to ₹1,99,853 cr before recovering suggests no demand surge. Passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY are falling for two consecutive months (from 26.1%), while two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY rebounded sharply — the classic urban-rural split where mass-market rural demand recovers faster than urban discretionary. Commercial vehicle sales at 12.6% YoY, falling two straight months, are the proxy to watch for freight and capex confidence.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit; 9.9%→17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY), now at 57th percentile. Services credit surging at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile), rising 2 straight months.","implication":"The deposit acceleration masks structural stress: banks are chasing credit growth via wholesale funding and NBFC partnerships. Overweight private banks with CASA ratios >45% and deposit-to-liability ratios >70% — they can poach retail deposits. Underweight NBFCs with wholesale funding >30% of liabilities; their funding costs will spike if RBI tightens liquidity. Watch for RBI to signal deposit-friendly measures (higher savings rates, CRR cuts) within 6 weeks. Avoid small-cap lenders entirely.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level; historically, ratios >85% preceded NBFC stress (2018–19). The divergence in growth rates is the real signal — it suggests credit demand is outpacing organic deposit mobilisation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadens Into Services","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (52nd percentile), up from 16.1% YoY. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile), up from 75.6%. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) — the highest in the dataset — rising 2 consecutive months (22.9%→24.3%). Agriculture credit at 17.2% YoY (78th percentile), also rising 2 straight months. Vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY (68th percentile), up from 8.7% YoY.","implication":"The capex cycle is no longer confined to manufacturing; services (IT, telecom, logistics) and agriculture are now borrowing aggressively. This is late-cycle behaviour — it signals confidence but also rising leverage. Overweight capital goods, cement, and steel stocks; they will see order book acceleration in Q4. Rotate into services infrastructure plays (data centres, logistics parks, telecom towers) — these are the new capex beneficiaries. Avoid consumer discretionary; capex-driven growth crowds out consumption.","pct_10y":77,"pct_note":"Services credit at 79th percentile is the highest in a decade; this breadth of capex (manufacturing, services, agri) last occurred in 2021–22 before the 2023 slowdown. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is sustainable but leaves little room for demand shocks.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Momentum Masks Affluent Rotation","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile), rising 3 consecutive months (₹29,845→₹31,961→₹32,297→₹32,490 cr / month). SIP accounts at 10.0646 mn (2nd percentile, historically low). SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (89th percentile). Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (80th percentile), up from ₹29,329 cr / month. DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile). FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile — outflows).","implication":"SIP inflows are at record highs, but account growth is stalled — average ticket size is rising sharply. This is affluent money entering via SIPs, not mass retail. Domestic institutions are the sole bid; FIIs are net sellers. Overweight large-cap, dividend-paying stocks (Nifty 50 constituents) where DIIs are concentrated. Avoid mid-cap and small-cap — they lack institutional support. The SIP story is real, but it's a wealth-concentration play, not a retail democratisation story.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile are at decade highs, but SIP accounts at 2nd percentile suggest the base is shrinking — a sign of consolidation into larger accounts. This divergence last occurred in 2021 before the 2022 correction.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI Pause","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, 10-year high), up from 20.05% YoY. Brent crude at $109.86/bbl (76th percentile), up from $105.5/bbl 2 months ago. WTI at $99.02/bbl (82nd percentile). CPI headline at 5.54% YoY (52nd percentile), up from 4.83% YoY. Food inflation at 7.74% YoY (57th percentile), rising 2 consecutive months (5.52%→7.74%). WPI at 9.92% YoY (67th percentile), up from 9.78% YoY.","implication":"Fuel and food inflation are now the dominant drivers of headline CPI. RBI's 5.1% inflation forecast (53rd percentile) is at risk of being breached if Brent stays >$105/bbl. The 5.25% repo rate is no longer accommodative in real terms. Position for a potential RBI rate hike in Q4 FY26 if CPI prints >5.8% in the next 2 months. Hedge long equity positions with long-duration bonds (10-year yields at 5.1%, 92nd percentile). Avoid refiners and power utilities; margin compression is imminent.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is the highest in the dataset's history. This level of energy price shock last preceded RBI tightening in 2022 and 2023. If Brent sustains >$110/bbl, CPI will breach 6% within 2 months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"BOJ Tightening Unwinds Carry Trades","data_text":"BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, 10-year high), up from 1% p.a., rising 2 consecutive months (0.75%→1%→1.25%). US 10-year Treasury yield at 5.1% (92nd percentile), down from 5.19% but still elevated. Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (68th percentile), up from 3.63% p.a. ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (63rd percentile), up from 2.25% p.a. US PMI composite at 58.4 index (91st percentile), rising 2 consecutive months (56→58.4). Global PMI composite at 54.3 index (84th percentile).","implication":"The BOJ's rate hike to 1.25% is the most hawkish signal in the dataset. Yen carry trades are unwinding — this will pressure INR and other EM currencies. US growth remains robust (PMI 58.4), but the Fed is unlikely to cut rates aggressively. The 5.1% US 10-year yield is a ceiling for EM bond yields; India's 10-year will struggle to fall below 6.5%. Reduce leverage in EM portfolios. Overweight INR hedges (long USD calls, short INR forwards). Avoid duration plays in Indian bonds; the carry is insufficient.","pct_10y":100,"pct_note":"BOJ at 100th percentile is a structural shift — the first rate hike in years signals the end of ultra-loose policy. This last occurred in 2015 before the 2015–16 EM crisis. Global PMI at 84th percentile suggests synchronized growth, which typically precedes synchronized tightening.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakness Accelerates Despite Inflows","data_text":"INR at 95.24 ₹/USD (89th percentile, 10-year high weakness), up from 94.96 ₹/USD. Recent trend: 96.15→95.24→96.15→97.09→96.15→95.24 (volatile, 2 of last 5 months weaker). FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile — outflows). DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile — strong inflows). India VIX at 14.025 index (9th percentile, very low volatility). US VIX at 19.99 index (15th percentile, elevated). DXY at 101.779 index (54th percentile).","implication":"INR is weakening despite strong DII inflows — this suggests FII outflows are structural, not cyclical. The 89th percentile weakness is a red flag. RBI is likely intervening to slow the depreciation, but reserves are being deployed. If FII outflows accelerate (watch for >-₹60,000 cr / month), INR could breach 97 within 6 weeks. Overweight INR hedges (long USD calls, short INR forwards). Avoid import-heavy sectors (autos, pharma); their margins will compress. Overweight exporters (IT, textiles, pharma APIs) — they benefit from INR weakness.","pct_10y":89,"pct_note":"INR at 89th percentile weakness is the highest in the dataset. This level of depreciation last occurred in 2022–23 before RBI's aggressive intervention. The divergence between DII inflows and FII outflows suggests foreign investors are rotating out of India.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Rents Surge While Vacancy Rises","data_text":"Bengaluru office rent at ₹163/sqft/mo (95th percentile, 10-year high), up from ₹148/sqft/mo. Recent trend: 102→103→163→100.6→103.6→109 (spike to 163 is anomalous). Office absorption at 14.1 mn sq ft / quarter (7th percentile, historically weak), up from 11.2 mn sq ft / quarter. Office vacancy at 14.37% vacant (41st percentile), up from 13.74%. Nifty IT index flat (recent: 22520→22363→22722→22623→22997→23146, up 3 of 5 but no momentum). Bank Nifty at 55,844 index (92nd percentile, near all-time highs).","implication":"Bengaluru office rents are spiking despite rising vacancy — this is a GCC (Global Capability Centre) phenomenon, not traditional IT services demand. Multinational tech companies (Google, Microsoft, Amazon) are consolidating into premium Grade-A buildings, while legacy IT services firms are shedding space. This decoupling is a leading indicator: GCCs are hiring engineers for AI/ML and cloud, not traditional IT services. The IT stock proxy (Nifty IT flat) is missing this structural shift. Overweight IT infrastructure plays (data centres, logistics parks) and underweight traditional IT services. The office market is bifurcating — premium rents for GCCs, distress for legacy IT parks. This is a 12-month leading indicator of IT services margin compression.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Bengaluru rents at 95th percentile with absorption at 7th percentile is a rare divergence — it signals a quality-driven market, not a quantity-driven one. This last occurred in 2019–20 before the COVID office exodus. The current spike suggests a structural reallocation, not cyclical demand.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP Headline — Services Carry What Goods Cannot

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY (64th percentile) sits 110bps above the RBI's own forecast of 6.7% YoY — a gap that deflator assumptions explain more convincingly than real output.
  • PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) and IIP Capital Goods at 16.9% YoY confirm expansion, but core sector at 4.8% YoY (down from 5.0%) signals the goods economy is losing pace.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY rebounded sharply while passenger vehicle sales fell to 7.9% YoY for two consecutive months — rural mass-market recovering faster than urban discretionary.
  • But commercial vehicle sales at 12.6% YoY, falling two straight months, are the freight proxy that contradicts the capex optimism.

The tension: Headline GDP and PMI signal broad expansion; core sector deceleration and falling CV sales suggest the goods economy is not confirming what the services surveys imply.

Bottom line: Watch CV sales and core sector for two more months — if both stay below 5% YoY, the GDP-GVA gap will widen and the 7.8% print will require a deflator explanation.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Re-acceleration Meets BOJ Tightening — EM Caught in the Crossfire

The facts:

  • US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile), rising two consecutive months, signals genuine re-acceleration — but US GDP SAAR at 2.2% SAAR (50th percentile) has not confirmed it yet.
  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, 10-year high), rising three consecutive months, is unwinding yen carry trades that funded EM positioning — including India.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (92nd percentile), down from 5.19%, offers a brief reprieve — but US CPI at 3.72% YoY, rising three consecutive months, keeps the Fed from cutting.
  • But China GDP at 4.4% YoY (46th percentile) with PMI Composite at 52.1 prevents any commodity reflation from sustaining — Brent at $109.86/bbl is a supply story, not a demand story.

The tension: DM surveys price re-acceleration; BOJ tightening and sticky US inflation mean the rate environment that supported EM carry trades is structurally tighter, not temporarily so.

Bottom line: BOJ at 1.25% p.a. is the underpriced tail risk — watch the next BOJ meeting for a fourth consecutive hike, which would force EM carry unwind within 30–60 days.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Autopilot Absorbs FII Exit — But the Margin Is Narrowing

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile), rising three consecutive months, and DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) are absorbing the FII exit.
  • But FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) represents near-complete DII offset — one more month of FII selling at this scale exhausts the cushion.
  • SIP accounts at 10.06 mn (2nd percentile historically) signal the account base is thin — inflow growth is ticket-size inflation among existing investors, not new retail participation.
  • NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile) confirm asset managers are not launching — the smart money is not adding new product risk at current valuations.

The tension: Headline SIP numbers suggest retail resilience; the account base percentile and NFO drought reveal that inflow growth is concentrated and fragile, not broad-based.

Bottom line: If FII outflows sustain above ₹40,000 cr / month for a third consecutive month, DII absorption will require SIP ticket sizes to rise further — a structurally unstable equilibrium.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Bank Nifty at All-Time Highs — REITs Disagree With the Narrative

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases jumped to 20% (from 10%, +10 pp), with NRI share within premium/luxury at 25%; remittances at $73 bn (12.8% YoY) are the funding source.
  • Hyderabad leads city momentum with sales 15% YoY and launches 120% YoY; NCR sales turned negative at -1% YoY — the two-speed residential market is widening.
  • Bank Nifty at 55,844 (92nd percentile) prices a clean credit cycle; but Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, and Brookfield at ₹263/unit are all down sharply from prior prints.
  • But office absorption at 14.1 mn sq ft / quarter (7th percentile) with vacancy at 14.37% vacant — and Bengaluru rent at ₹163/sqft/mo (95th percentile) that is anomalous against a trend of ₹100–109 — signals a rent spike that absorption data does not support.

The tension: Bank Nifty prices credit cycle perfection; REIT unit prices and 7th-percentile office absorption tell a different story about the commercial real estate demand that underpins BFSI and IT sector confidence.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until absorption sustains above 18 mn sq ft / quarter for two consecutive quarters — the Bengaluru rent spike is a data anomaly, not a trend.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Detonator — Crude Holds the Match

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, 10-year high) with Brent at $109.86/bbl — every $10 adds ~$15 bn to India's import bill, widens CAD by ~40bps, and feeds CPI with a two-quarter lag.
  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) rising three consecutive months — yen carry unwind is not priced into India VIX at 14.0 (9th percentile), which makes hedges historically cheap.
  • CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits (73rd percentile) with credit at 19.4% YoY vs deposits at 17.8% YoY — services credit at 24.3% YoY is the segment most exposed to a risk-weight circular.
  • India VIX at 14.0 (9th percentile) while US VIX at 19.99 (15th percentile) — the divergence between domestic complacency and global stress is at an extreme that historically closes violently, not gradually.

The tension: Domestic volatility pricing implies India is insulated from global stress; the crude, BOJ, and credit-deposit data all point to transmission channels that are open and underpriced.

Bottom line: Watch Brent this week — a close above $112/bbl forces the RBI's hand on the pause and triggers the CAD-INR-CPI chain that the market is not positioned for.

"}
